title: Will Suncor's Refining Strength Continue to Drive Cash Flow? - The Globe and Mail
content: Suncor Energy Inc. SU continues to benefit from its integrated refining operations, supported by stronger refining margins, high utilization and growing refined product sales. The company's downstream business has become a significant contributor to cash generation, raising expectations about its ability to sustain profitability. In the third quarter of 2026, Suncor's Refining and Marketing segment generated C$3.61 billion in adjusted funds from operations, compared with C$1.22 billion a year earlier. Segment free funds flow increased to C$3.29 billion from C$926 million, reflecting favorable refining conditions. Higher cracking margins were a major contributor to the improvement. Operational performance remained encouraging, with refinery utilization reaching 95% and crude throughput of approximately 488,000 barrels per day. Refined product sales increased to a third-quarter record of nearly 677,000 barrels per day from approximately 647,000 barrels a year earlier. Previous debottlenecking initiatives expanded high-value export capacity, while stronger domestic retail sales supported performance. Suncor's integrated operations provide another advantage. The Edmonton refinery's direct connection to oil sands production improves feedstock flexibility and operational efficiency. This integration helped maintain refinery throughput during planned maintenance, while logistics capabilities largely offset supply disruptions in Eastern Canada. Looking ahead, Suncor's 511,000-barrel-per-day refining network, diverse crude sourcing and access to high-value markets support its cash generation potential. However, sustaining the recent momentum will depend on refining margins, product demand and continued operational reliability. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM also benefited from favorable refining conditions in the third quarter of 2026. The company's Energy Products earnings increased to $7.17 billion from $1.84 billion a year earlier. ExxonMobil achieved 100% crude unit utilization at the U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, reflecting strong operational performance and its ability to capture favorable margins. Chevron Corporation CVX reported downstream earnings of $4.93 billion, compared with $1.14 billion a year earlier, supported by higher refined product margins. The company's U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput of 1.09 million barrels per day, with utilization approaching 98%. Chevron's reliable refining operations highlight its ability to benefit from favorable market conditions. Suncor's shares have gained 67.5% over the past year, outperforming ExxonMobil's 46.3% increase and Chevron's 39.7% rise. SU's stronger share-price performance reflects investor interest in its integrated operations, improved cash generation and shareholder returns. The gains also highlight growing confidence in the company's ability to sustain profitability across its upstream and downstream businesses. Suncor appears attractively valued compared with its integrated energy peers. The stock trades at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 9.59, below ExxonMobil’s 13.26 and Chevron’s 12.45. This suggests that investors can gain exposure to Suncor’s expected earnings at a lower price than those of its larger peers. The valuation discount, combined with solid refining operations and healthy cash generation, adds to the stock’s investment appeal. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for Suncor's EPS has increased 18.54% for 2026 and 11.31% for 2027. The current estimates stand at $8.76 per share for 2026 and $7.28 for 2027. These upward revisions indicate improving analyst expectations for Suncor's earnings performance, supported by its integrated business model and favorable operating conditions. Suncor's strong refining performance, growing cash flow and integrated operations support its outlook. The stock’s attractive valuation relative to peers and upward earnings estimate revisions further strengthen its investment appeal, despite refining margin volatility. Lower realised prices weighed on revenue, and an accelerated entitlement effect in Guyana reduced the company's share of production under the terms of the production sharing contract. Entitlement mechanics can confuse casual observers. Under many production sharing agreements, the host government and partners recover costs first, and as those costs are repaid the operator's share of barrels can shift. The accelerated effect in the latest quarter means a portion of the expected shift arrived earlier than modelled, which trims posted earnings without changing the physical flow of oil from the Stabroek block. title: IMF Projects 22.3% GDP Growth For Guyana As ExxonMobil's (NYSE: XOM) Uaru Project Unlocks New Supply Capacity - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 5, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis Few economies anywhere in the world are expanding at the pace Guyana is, with the International Monetary Fund projecting GDP growth of 22.3% for the country in 2026. The driver behind that extraordinary figure is an oil sector that has transformed this small South American nation into one of the most closely watched energy stories on the planet. Guyana is closing in on a production milestone of one million barrels per day, a threshold that would have seemed unimaginable for the country just a decade ago. Adding further momentum to that trajectory is ExxonMobil’s (NYSE: XOM) Uaru project, which is expected to bring an additional 250,000 barrels per day of production capacity online. That incremental supply is significant not just for Guyana’s economy, but for energy markets that are increasingly anxious about concentration risk in global oil flows. Tensions across the Middle East have renewed concerns about the security of shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most critical chokepoints for crude oil transit. A disruption to that corridor would send shockwaves through energy markets, tightening supply precisely when major economies are already navigating inflationary pressures and uneven growth. Guyana’s expanding export capacity offers a geographically distinct alternative, with Atlantic Basin crude routes that bypass the vulnerabilities associated with Gulf shipping lanes entirely. The diversification argument has gained traction among energy analysts and policymakers who view Western Hemisphere production growth as a structural buffer against Middle Eastern supply shocks. For Guyana itself, the stakes extend well beyond barrels and benchmarks, with oil revenues reshaping public finances, infrastructure investment, and the country’s longer-term development outlook. The IMF’s 22.3% growth forecast places Guyana in a category virtually alone among its peers, reflecting how rapidly petroleum receipts are flowing into the broader economy. Exxon’s continued capital commitment through projects like Uaru signals that the investment cycle driving this boom still has considerable runway ahead, with capacity expansions compounding on one another. Whether Guyana’s institutions can manage that pace of wealth accumulation responsibly remains an open question, but the near-term production picture points firmly upward. For global energy markets contending with supply uncertainty, the emergence of a credible, scalable Atlantic producer may prove to be one of the more consequential developments of the decade. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

title: Is Exxon Mobil Stock Still Worth Owning After Its Quarter? - Trefis

Shares of Exxon Mobil (XOM) rose 2.2% on October 30, 2026, the day it reported fiscal Q3 2026 results, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8%. The stock retreated by November 4, trading 7.6% below its close on the eve of the report. Shareholders own Exxon for profits and payouts that endure through the oil cycle, and its profit just jumped. So is that higher profit Exxon’s own, or the market’s? So far, more of it looks like the market’s. Exxon earned $15.4 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, against $7.55 billion a year earlier. The company earned $4.18 billion in fiscal Q1 2026, meaning the whole step up arrived in the last two quarters. Fiscal Q2 2026 profit was already $14.5 billion. Management said a lack of supply led to tight markets and higher prices. Its guess was that fuel markets would not get back closer to normal until well through 2027, or longer. Chevron and ConocoPhillips shares rose by similar amounts on report day, so the quarter did little to set Exxon apart from its peers. Exxon does have gains of its own. Management cited $16.9 billion of structural cost savings since 2019. Setting aside Middle East impacts, executives said production rose from a year earlier, helped by growth in the Permian and Guyana. Those savings accumulated over several years, while the higher profit has lasted just two quarters. Exxon’s payouts hold up so far. The company returned $9.4 billion to holders through dividends and buybacks in fiscal Q3 2026, against $18.5 billion of free cash flow. Management raised the dividend per share 4%, marking its 44th straight year of increases. The company also plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, assuming reasonable market conditions. Exxon carries light debt as well, at 4.9% of its market value against 19.2% for the S&P 500. Profit fell by more than a third, and the payouts kept going. Exxon earned $51.9 billion in the twelve months to September 2022, and $30.0 billion in the twelve months to September 2025. During that leaner year, free cash flow of $23.8 billion landed only a little above the $20.7 billion Exxon spent on buybacks alone. Total payouts of $37.9 billion ran well above free cash flow with $17.2 billion of dividends included. Management said that at the bottom of the cycle, Exxon does not pull back from its commitment to holders and uses the balance sheet to make up the difference. The company has less cash to draw on now, holding $12.2 billion at the end of September 2026, against $30.4 billion four years earlier. Apart from buybacks, management left its 2027 plan to a later date. The company said it will confirm key 2027 planning figures in a press release later in fiscal Q4 2026, offering more detail on its fourth-quarter call in January. Cash flow covered Exxon’s payouts in fiscal Q3 2026, while the company has held its higher profit for only two quarters. Its quarterly profit at the fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM - Get Free Report) had its price target upped by research analysts at TD Cowen  from $180.00 to $193.00 in a research note issued to investors on Wednesday, Benzinga reports. The firm currently has a "buy" rating on the oil and gas company's stock. TD Cowen's price objective would indicate a potential upside of 14.25% from the company's current price. Other equities analysts have also recently issued research reports about the stock. William Blair started coverage on shares of ExxonMobil in a research note on Wednesday, October 28th. They issued a "market perform" rating on the stock. Wall Street Zen upgraded ExxonMobil from a "hold" rating to a "buy" rating in a research report on Saturday, October 24th. Mizuho lowered their price target on shares of ExxonMobil from $175.00 to $170.00 and set a "neutral" rating for the company in a report on Thursday, July 9th. BNP Paribas Exane decreased their price objective on shares of ExxonMobil from $165.00 to $155.00 and set a "neutral" rating for the company in a research note on Friday, July 17th. Finally, Zacks Research upgraded shares of ExxonMobil from a "hold" rating to a "strong-buy" rating in a research note on Monday, October 19th. One research analyst has rated the stock with a Strong Buy rating, eleven have given a Buy rating, thirteen have assigned a Hold rating and one has given a Sell rating to the company. According to data from MarketBeat, the company presently has a consensus rating of "Hold" and a consensus target price of $169.87. The company has a current ratio of 1.19, a quick ratio of 0.92 and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.11. ExxonMobil has a 12 month low of $113.64 and a 12 month high of $188.50. The business's 50 day moving average price is $168.33 and its 200 day moving average price is $154.86. The company has a market cap of $700.21 billion, a price-to-earnings ratio of 17.36, a price-to-earnings-growth ratio of 0.90 and a beta of 0.16. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM - Get Free Report) last announced its earnings results on Friday, October 30th. The oil and gas company reported $4.23 earnings per share (EPS) for the quarter, beating the consensus estimate of $4.12 by $0.11. The firm had revenue of $110.50 billion during the quarter, compared to analyst estimates of $104.89 billion. ExxonMobil had a return on equity of 16.63% and a net margin of 10.24%. During the same period last year, the firm posted $1.88 EPS.  On average, equities research analysts predict that ExxonMobil will post 13.61 EPS for the current year. GQG Partners LLC now owns 16,877,523 shares of the oil and gas company's stock valued at $2,307,497,000 after purchasing an additional 10,214,420 shares during the last quarter. title: Why ExxonMobil and Chevron Reminded Investors to Keep it Simple - MarketBeat
content:
Some of 2026's best large-cap stories didn't come from Silicon Valley. They came from Texas. At the market close on Nov. 3, Chevron Corp. NYSE: CVX was up more than 46% over the past year. ExxonMobil NYSE: XOM has had an even more impressive run, up nearly 56%. Both stocks also pay dividends that keep growing. Chevron yields about 3% and has raised its payout for 38 straight years. ExxonMobil's streak of annual dividend increases now stands at 42 years with a yield of around 2.3%. Yet many investors spent the year looking elsewhere. Capital chased artificial intelligence (AI) and the technology names tied to it. Energy stocks were treated as a trade on oil prices rather than on the businesses themselves. The trade seemed simple: when crude cools off, so will these stocks. Third-quarter results, released by Chevron and ExxonMobil on Oct. 30, challenge that view. Higher prices helped. But refining strength, cost discipline and balance sheet repair did much of the work. Both companies also absorbed accounting headwinds that should reverse. That sets up a case for further upside, even after a big year. Chevron reported adjusted earnings of $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. That's up from $1.85 per share a year ago. Brent crude averaged $97 per barrel versus $69, lifting upstream results. But the bigger swing came from refining. Downstream earnings jumped to $4.9 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier. Chevron's U.S. refineries processed a record 1.09 million barrels per day. Crude unit utilization reached nearly 98%. That matters because refining profits depend on margins, not just crude prices. Strong margins offset a 109,000 barrel-per-day drop in international production. Chevron tied that decline to price-driven entitlement effects and the Middle East conflict. Cash flow tells the rest of the story. Chevron generated $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow. It paid $3.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $2.5 billion of stock. It still cut total debt by $3.5 billion. Net debt fell $7.8 billion in the quarter alone. Management also laid out a growth path. Chevron's Venezuelan joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over five years. The company says that could more than double production there. In the Bakken, new agreements should cut midstream costs by roughly 50%. Both moves aim to improve returns per barrel, not just add volume. ExxonMobil posted adjusted earnings of $17.5 billion, or $4.23 per share. That compares with $3.52 per share in the second quarter. GAAP earnings came in at $3.72 per share. Operating cash flow totaled $25.7 billion, and free cash flow reached $19.1 billion. Like Chevron, ExxonMobil leaned on refining. Adjusted Energy Products earnings more than doubled from the prior quarter to $9.1 billion. Its U.S. Gulf Coast refineries ran at 100% crude unit utilization. Meanwhile, upstream earnings fell on lower prices and a Guyana entitlement impact. The integrated model did exactly what it was built to do. CEO Darren Woods made a point investors should note. He described the gains as lasting improvements, not just the product of favorable pricing. ExxonMobil estimates its structural cost savings at $16.9 billion since 2019. Lower costs reduce the oil price needed to keep earnings and dividends growing. Shareholders are getting paid along the way. ExxonMobil returned $9.4 billion in the quarter, including $5.1 billion in buybacks. It plans $20 billion in repurchases for 2027. It also declared a $1.07 quarterly dividend. Net debt has fallen by nearly $11 billion so far this year. Both reports carried a detail that's easy to miss. Rising oil prices created "timing effects" that reduced reported earnings. These come mainly from marking derivatives to market before physical barrels are delivered. Chevron absorbed $1.58 billion in negative timing effects. ExxonMobil's hit totaled roughly $2.5 billion. ExxonMobil notes these impacts are expected to unwind in later periods. In other words, part of the third quarter's profit was deferred, not lost. If prices stabilize, that reversal could boost results in the coming quarters. It's a potential catalyst many investors may not be watching. None of this makes these stocks completely safe. Future results still depend heavily on commodity prices and refining margins. Both are elevated partly because of the Middle East conflict. If supply disruptions ease, margins could compress quickly. Chevron's total production also slipped from a year ago, which bears watching. Valuation is less forgiving after a 50% run. Investors buying now are paying for continued strength. That makes execution over the next few quarters more important, not less. The lesson from this quarter isn't complicated. Two of the world's largest energy companies are generating enormous amounts of cash. They're cutting debt, buying back stock, and raising dividends. And they're doing it with growing help from refining and cost cuts, not just oil prices. Investors who chased complexity this year may have overlooked that simplicity. For those still on the sidelines, the latest results suggest the story isn't finished. Patient, income-focused investors may find that keeping it simple still pays.  reported third-quarter earnings that topped analyst estimates, helped by record refining performance and continued production growth in its most important oil fields. For readers following US Oil and Gas Stocks, the results showed how the company's integrated model can perform in a volatile energy market. Geopolitical tension, including conflicts affecting energy supply, has pushed fuel prices higher this year. That backdrop supported refining profits, while the company's own cost discipline and project execution helped lift cash generation. The standout performer was the energy products segment, which includes refining. Earnings in this business more than doubled from the previous quarter, driven by higher margins and strong operations. Global refining utilisation reached a record, with US Gulf Coast crude units running close to full capacity. Refining profits tend to rise when fuel demand is strong and supply is tight. With gasoline and diesel prices elevated, ExxonMobil's large refining network was well positioned to benefit. Chemical product earnings declined as margins weakened, reflecting softer industrial demand and new global capacity. Specialty products, which include lubricants and base stocks, improved on better margins. Together, these segments show the diversity of the company's earnings base. Upstream earnings fell from the previous quarter, reflecting lower crude prices during the period and production entitlement effects in Guyana. Overall output stayed broadly stable. Even so, the long-term growth story in upstream remains strong. Guyana's Stabroek block surpassed a major cumulative production milestone just over a decade after discovery, described as the fastest ramp of any major offshore development. The Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico also continued to deliver strong volumes. Management pointed to large structural cost savings achieved over recent years, which have strengthened earnings across commodity cycles. Automation is expanding in the Permian, with automated drilling rigs expected to cover a growing share of the fleet in coming years. The company also highlighted technology transfer between businesses. Refining expertise helped develop a lighter material used in drilling, an example of how integration can create advantages that standalone producers may lack. ExxonMobil is taking over operatorship of the Papua LNG project and increasing its stake, reinforcing its position in liquefied natural gas. LNG demand is expected to grow as countries look for cleaner alternatives to coal and secure energy supplies. In carbon capture, the company started another operation for an outside customer and gained approval for a new storage project. These businesses remain small but offer long-term options as industrial customers seek to reduce emissions. Strong cash flow supported continued dividends and share repurchases. The company is in its fifth decade of consecutive annual dividend increases and confirmed plans to keep repurchases at a similar pace next year. Net debt also declined during the quarter, strengthening an already solid balance sheet. This combination of rising dividends and repurchases is a key reason many income-focused investors follow the stock, particularly in a market where few large companies offer such a long payout record. ExxonMobil's strategy rests on investing in advantaged assets that remain profitable even when oil prices fall. Guyana and the Permian are central to that approach because they combine large resources with relatively low production costs. LNG projects add long-term contracted cash flows that are less sensitive to short-term price swings. Management has also emphasised capital discipline. Rather than spending heavily when prices are high, the company aims to keep investment steady and return excess cash to investors. That consistency has supported confidence in the dividend through several energy cycles. Refining and chemicals give the company a natural hedge. When crude prices fall, refining margins may improve because input costs drop, partly cushioning the impact on upstream earnings. This balance is a key reason large integrated companies are viewed as more resilient than pure producers. Energy prices remain volatile and tied to geopolitics, supply decisions by major producers and economic growth. Refining margins can fall quickly if demand weakens or new capacity arrives. Regulatory and climate policies also shape long-term investment decisions. As a heavyweight member of the NYSE Composite, ExxonMobil remains a bellwether for the US energy sector. The coming quarters will test whether refining strength persists and whether upstream growth in Guyana and the Permian continues on schedule. For now, the quarter highlights a company using its scale, integration and cost control to deliver solid results even as individual segments move in different directions. Low-cost production remains a focus across the portfolio. By concentrating capital on the most profitable barrels and steadily lowering break-even levels, ExxonMobil aims to keep generating cash even if prices fall sharply from current levels, a priority that management has repeated throughout the year. title: Will ExxonMobil's 100,000-BPD Diesel Expansion Boost Refining Profit? - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM is focusing on expanding its refining operations to increase the production of higher-value fuels, particularly diesel, and strengthen long-term profitability. The company expects its investments across U.S. refineries to increase distillate production by another 100,000 barrels per day (BPD). This expansion is part of XOM's broader strategy to improve its product mix and enhance earnings and cash flow. According to media reports citing ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods' Oct. 30, 2026, CNBC interview, the company plans to allocate approximately 10% of its more than $100 billion capital investment program for 2027-2030 toward refining operations, representing roughly $10 billion in planned spending. The integrated energy giant has already invested around $17 billion in refining since 2019, increasing crude processing capacity by nearly 10% over the period. Projects such as the Beaumont refinery expansion have contributed to a roughly 40% increase in U.S. Gulf Coast distillate production, while ongoing work at Baytown is aimed at expanding output. Beyond capacity additions, XOM has reduced refinery turnaround costs by about 30%, reflecting improved operational efficiency. The expansion comes as global refining capacity constraints have tightened fuel supplies and supported stronger refining margins. XOM's expanded trading and optimization capabilities allow it to secure advantaged feedstocks and direct refined products to higher-value markets. The planned increase in diesel production, combined with ongoing investments and improved operating efficiency, is expected to enhance ExxonMobil's earnings and cash flow, although profitability remains dependent on refining market conditions. The focus on increasing higher-value fuel production extends beyond ExxonMobil, with Valero Energy Corporation VLO and Marathon Petroleum Corporation MPC investing in refining efficiency and product optimization. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Valero Energy highlighted improvements in its product mix following the completion of the $230 million St. Charles refinery optimization project. Meanwhile, Marathon Petroleum emphasized that investments at its Garyville and Robinson facilities have enhanced operating flexibility and supported higher distillate yields. While VLO is working to strengthen its refining competitiveness through operational improvements, MPC remains focused on optimizing its refining network to support profitability. ExxonMobil's shares have gained 56% over the past year compared with the industry’s 51.1% growth.
